items.title: 71542_Bill Coleman autobiographical manuscript
items.q: The two best known orchestras amongst the Negro musicians were Jack Jackson's orchestra who had come on the scene after I had left Cincinnati

ctx.x: I figured that I would stay in Cincinnati long enough to get a divorce which was much easier to do there than it was in New York. So Beezie and I packed our few belongings and left the Apple by bus one afternoon and arrived in Cincinnati the next day. We lived with my father who had two rooms on Outter Street near Court Street. My mother was living on Court Street not far from my father, so I saw her every day. My brother was living with my father also.

I was not in town very long before all the musicians knew I was there. The two best known orchestras amongst the Negro musicians were Jack Jackson's orchestra who had come on the scene after I had left Cincinnati, and Clarence Page who was the best known and most popular orchestra. Clarence contacted me a few days after I arrived and I started working with him doing one-night stands in Kentucky, West Virginia and Ohio.

Harl "Inky" Tremble whom I had known for many years played alto sax and was director of the band because Clarence prefered to sit and play tenor. Inky was a nice front man on the style of Cecil Scott, and he was always inventing names for people and things that already had a name. He was the one that started calling Melvin Oliver, "Sy" which was a short name of psychology. When Sy joined Zack White's band, Inky was also in the band.
